newsitem.title: USA: HOLLYWOOD ASKS: who's Billy Bob?.
newsitem.headline: HOLLYWOOD ASKS: who's Billy Bob?.

text.p: That was the reaction two weeks ago when Billy Bob Thornton was nominated for best actor in this year's Academy Awards. Now America is learning that Thornton may be a force to reckon with come Oscar night because the critics are in love with the oddball "Sling Blade," which he wrote and directed as well as starring.

The film tells the story of a loner named Carl who is released after spending 20 years in an institution for the criminally insane where he was confined at the age of 12 for killing his mother and her younger lover with a sling blade, a scythe-like knife used to cut weeds.

Thornton plays the slow, nearly retarded Carl with an eerie, unforgettable speech pattern that is part gravel, part menace. "He's like an older country man in lots of ways: The walk, the language," said Thornton, 41, who "based that on guys like my great-grandfather."

When Carl returns to his sleepy Arkansas hometown, he befriends a young boy who needs protection from his mother's abusive boyfriend, played by country and western singer Dwight Yoakum. "Sling Blade" then becomes a story of murder and redemption.
A nearly unrecognizable, pot-bellied John Ritter is featured as the mother's gay best friend.

One reason so few knew about Thornton is that the film opened only in Los Angeles and New York for Oscar-qualifying runs last year. The week the nominations were announced "Sling Blade" was playing in only 16 cities in the United States. The weekend after, it moved into 40 markets. With the Oscar attention -- Thornton was also nominated for Best Screenplay Adaptation -- "Sling Blade" is certain to be seen.

Thornton, who refuses to fly, heard about his nomination while on a train from New York to Los Angeles. "I'd been in New York doing David Letterman and all those things," he said. He was on his cellular phone when his call waiting beeped and he was connected to L.A. disc jockeys Mark and Bryan.
"They asked me on the air on the radio show, 'How do you feel?' 'Feel about what?' I said. I didn't know about the nomination until they told me!"

An Arkansas native, Thornton has been in Los Angeles for 16 years, working as an actor and screenwriter. Prior to "Sling Blade" he was praised for his screenplays for "One False Move," a nasty little 1992 film noir that established Carl Franklin ("The Devil in a Blue Dress") as a major Hollywood director, and last year's "A Family Thing," with James Earl Jones and Robert Duvall.

If these are heady times, the hard times were only 12 years ago. Before his acting career began, Thornton nearly starved to death. But he insists he did not, as one rumour had it, survive on canned dog food.

"This is the truth," he said. "I went for two weeks with a huge economy bag of raw potatoes but no cooking oil or anything. I would fry those potatoes in the skillet that came with the apartment I was in and they'd just smoke the place every night.

"That's what I was eating, these scorched potatoes, and my heart quit on me. It was an inflammation, what happens to people who are anorexic -- but in my case it was because I was starving to death," he said.

"(Soon after that) I started to get parts, thug number two on 'Matlock' and the bailiff on 'Divorce Court.' I got this little part in a movie, five lines as a railroad conductor in the '20s. I had a haircut like Carl's and I'm feeling bad about myself."

So Thornton went into his trailer, started making faces in the mirror -- and out came this voice talking bad about himself. It was right there, in a flash of inspiration, that Thornton improvised Carl's entire seven-minute monologue in the mirror.
"Afterwards, I put it exactly like that in this one-man show; Carl was one of four characters in this show."
